lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
- Cut the signal's daily turnover from 34% to 21% with a cost-aware position smoother, keeping 90% of gross returns and lowering estimated slippage by a third.
- Confirmed the forecast gain over the nested HAR-RV baseline with standard Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices.
- Joining 120 microstructure features point-in-time across six venues, deduplicating late prints and versioning each schema, built a feature store the team reused in two later projects.
- Annualized the signal's daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying it by 252 before reporting it to the desk.
- Documented the backtest assumptions, transaction-cost model and known failure regimes in the desk's research wiki, which the next intern cohort used to onboard in their first week.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Aug 2021
- Owned the lab's simulation pipeline on the shared cluster and the reproducibility checks other students relied on.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator that tightens the previous bound by a log factor; it is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.

- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation while maintaining the lab's shared cluster, organizing the weekly reading group and grading for two courses, which was downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Cut forecast error from 0.20 to 0.15, a 33% improvement, by adding realized-volatility features and an asymmetric loss.
- Improved the model's directional hit rate by 6% on 30 equity indices, from 52% to 58%, with a temporal convolutional model.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Placed 41st of 2,900 teams with a gradient-boosting ensemble on 300 engineered features, finishing in the top 2% of the private leaderboard.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Wrote the team's feature-selection script using permutation importance, trimming 900 candidate features to 300 without losing validation score.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: Multiplying a daily Sharpe ratio by 252 is mathematically wrong.
items.because: Under the standard convention, it is typically scaled by the square root of the number of trading days.

items.says: Verify that Sharpe figures elsewhere are annualized consistently.
items.because: The annualization error undermines confidence in the other performance figures.

items.says: Make sure the code link is a direct, working URL.
Make sure the contact information is current.
Consider adding a research area or dissertation focus.
items.because: It could strengthen the Ph.D. line’s fit for the roles being targeted.

items.says: Clarify whether the Sharpe change is the signal’s contribution to the desk book or a comparison between two backtests.
items.because: The signal’s effect on the desk book is unclear.

items.says: Specify whether the Sharpe ratio is annualized.
Define the out-of-sample period.
Define the cost assumptions behind the backtest.
Ensure the result is approved for disclosure.
Define what “90% of gross returns” refers to.
Explain how slippage was estimated.
Make the return, turnover and slippage comparisons use the same baseline and period.
Clarify what forecast was tested.
Clarify what the forecast “gain” means.
Consider the effect of overlapping observations or multiple comparisons on significance across 30 indices.
Do not treat the forecast comparison as necessarily supporting the trading-performance claim.
items.because: The test supports a forecast comparison, not necessarily the first bullet’s trading result.

items.says: The feature-store bullet has a malformed grammatical construction.
items.because: The opening “Joining” does not connect cleanly to the stated result.

items.says: Distinguish your feature-store work from the team’s.
Clarify whether the feature store was used in production or research.
Reword “used to onboard in their first week.”
items.because: It is awkward.

items.says: Substantiate the onboarding result or qualify the documentation’s role.
items.because: The claim may overstate that role.

items.says: Give the pipeline ownership and reproducibility checks more scope or a concrete outcome.
items.because: “Owned” and “relied on” are broad, making the bullet less informative than the research and teaching achievements.

items.says: Clarify your role in the variance-bound work.
Use the paper’s exact publication status.
Focus less on the work being “Section 3.”
items.because: That detail is less meaningful to most readers than the contribution and its status.

items.says: Clarify whether the 4.8/5 rating is a student evaluation and what it measures.
Give the period covered by the teaching rating if relevant.
Separate the R package achievement from the lab duties or prioritize the most relevant parts.
items.because: The bullet combines several different responsibilities.

items.says: Clarify that the 3,000 downloads refer to the package.
items.because: “Which” has an unclear referent.

items.says: Provide the source of the download count if available.
Specify the train/test split.
items.because: The evaluation setup should show that the result is genuinely out of sample.

items.says: Say whether the results are aggregated across indices.
items.because: The comparison should be reproducible and clearly defined.

items.says: Calling the change from 0.20 to 0.15 a 33% improvement is incorrect.
items.because: Measured against the starting value, it is a 25% reduction.

items.says: Name the forecast-error metric.
items.because: “Forecast error” does not identify what is measured.

items.says: Clarify the comparison baseline for adding realized-volatility features.
items.because: The preceding bullet already describes a model trained on those features.

items.says: The move from 52% to 58% is not a six-percent increase.
items.because: It is a six-percentage-point increase.

items.says: Define what direction is being predicted.
Say whether the hit rate uses the same out-of-sample period.
Avoid repeating the temporal convolutional model detail unless it adds distinct information.
items.because: The model is mentioned elsewhere.

items.says: Confirm that both “41st” and top 2% refer to the private leaderboard.
Use the competition’s exact official name if possible.
Do not present the smaller validation-to-leaderboard gap as proof that leakage was reduced.
items.because: A smaller gap does not by itself prove reduced leakage.

items.says: Clarify whether the preserved validation score was measured under time-grouped evaluation.
Avoid implying that leaderboard results guided feature selection.
Kafka is incorrectly grouped under programming languages.
items.because: It is a data-streaming tool rather than a programming language.

items.says: “Econometircs” is misspelled.
Make sure the broad listed methods are demonstrated by the experience or projects.
items.because: Broad terms are most useful when the résumé clearly demonstrates them.
